about: Pronunciation fixes for Liam (Kokoro am_onyx). The beat sheet's narration_text and the captions are never changed; these substitutions are applied only to the text sent to the voice. Started 2026-10-07 at Professor Bear's request; add an entry whenever a word is said wrong.
how_to_add: Add an entry with a regex that has a named group 'w' around the word to replace, the respelling in 'say', and at least one example with the phoneme string it must produce ('expect'). Run: python3 runtime/scripts/pronunciation.py --check. The check asks Kokoro's own phonemizer what it will say, so a respelling is verified without listening, though it still needs an ear on first use.

entries.note: Verb rih-KORD (ɹᵻkˈɔːɹd), not noun REK-erd (ɹˈɛkɚd). Kokoro defaults even 'Record its source' to the noun. Apply only to clear imperative or subject/modal/infinitive verb contexts with an object, leaving noun uses such as 'a record of', 'source record', and 'record player' untouched. Conservative patterns, not a general part-of-speech parser; add narrow contexts when needed. Authored narration and captions retain record. Requested 2026-10-08; preview awaits listening approval.

entries.note: Third-person verb 'records' (ri-KORDZ: 'a success statement records what was said'), not the noun REK-erdz ('record store'). Kokoro reads every 'records' as the noun. Applies only when 'records' is followed by an object clause opener (what, how, where, when, who, whether, the, its, their, each, every, all, a, an). Noun 'these records were written' is left alone. Authored narration and captions keep 'records'. Bear, 2026-10-09: 'records ... sounds like a record store; it should be record, the verb'.

examples.text: A success statement records what was said.

entries.note: Use first-syllable-stressed American PRAH-vuh-nuhns, not PROOV-nuhns. Kokoro's default phonemizer emits pɹˈuːvnəns for the normal spelling; doubling the v yields pɹˈɑːvənəns. Voice-only override requested by Professor Bear on 2026-10-08. Reference: https://dictionary.cambridge.org/pronunciation/english/provenance . Captions and authored narration retain provenance. Listening approval is still needed for the generated preview.

entries.note: Adjective LYVE (lˈaɪv), not the verb liv (lˈɪv). Bear, 2026-10-09: if something lives somewhere and is there, it is live; if it is online, it is live. Liam mixes the two. Covers: copula/state (is/was/now/already/still live), going/went/set/put live, 'live' before a noun (site, link, demo, data…), 'live on/at/in' + a place (GitHub, the web, the site, production, a URL), sentence-final 'live'. Verb uses stay: 'we live in', 'it lives on the server', 'to live'. Authored narration and captions retain live.

examples.text: The page is already live on GitHub.
The film is live at youtube.com.
The file lives on the server.

entries.note: 'polish' as in shine or finish (rhymes with 'wallish'), not the nationality 'Polish' (said 'POH-lish'). A capital P makes the voice choose the nationality, so the word is respelled everywhere except before words that make the nationality obvious. 'polished' is already right and is not touched.
Said 'NAH-mah-stay'; the voice reads it as 'NAM-ast' otherwise.
Plural of AI is 'A-eyes' (ay + eyes, like somebody's eyes), one smooth word. The old AI entry left 'A-Is', which Kokoro says as 'A-iz' / 'AIS'. Bear, 2026-10-09.
Narration spells the acronym 'A. I.' with periods; Kokoro then reads two letters with a pause. Joined, it is ay-eye with no break. Bear, 2026-10-09.

Sentence-final 'A. I.' keeps its full stop but loses the pause between the letters. 'A-I-.' (trailing hyphen) is what makes Kokoro say ay-eye as one unit before punctuation; plain 'A-I.' gives two separate stresses.

examples.text: You are not the A. I. Next.

entries.note: 'A. I.' directly before a comma or other mark: trailing hyphen keeps it one smooth unit.
Mid-sentence 'A. I.' read as one smooth 'ay-eye', not 'A' pause 'I'.

examples.text: An A. I. writes the code.

entries.note: Said as one quick word, 'ay-eye' with a single stress and no gap between the letters (phonemes ˈeɪaɪ). Earlier 'A.I.' put a full stop and two stresses in, which Professor Bear heard as a pause (2026-10-08). Plain 'AI' gives ˌeɪˈaɪ, also with no pause but a weaker first letter; 'A-I' keeps both letters clear. Needs an ear on first use.

examples.text: Conducting AI means the person directs.

entries.note: Verb liv (lˈɪv), the other half of Bear's 2026-10-09 rule: 'lives on the server', 'we live in the terminal'. Kokoro's default reads the verb as LYVE in these contexts. Matches live/lives/lived before a place or manner word, after a subject pronoun, or after 'to'. Runs after live-adjective, which has already respelled the adjective to 'lyve', so there is no clash.

examples.text: The file lives on the server.

entries.note: Bear, 2026-10-09: the Greek letter is pi as in apple pie (pˈaɪ). Lowercase or capitalised 'pi'/'Pi' only; all-caps PI is the principal investigator (see PI-caps). Kokoro already says pˈaɪ by default; this entry locks it in and is checked.

entries.note: Bear, 2026-10-09: all-caps PI is the principal investigator, said as the two letters P I (pˈiːˈaɪ), never pie. Also PIs.

entries.note: Plural of the all-caps principal investigator: 'PIs' → P-I's so Kokoro says pˈiːaɪz (the apostrophe is what makes the s read as a plural).

Northeastern's AI cluster. Kokoro reads AICR as 'acre'. Bear, 2026-10-11: say it ONE way, always - the four letters A-I-C-R (the alternative he allowed was 'Aker', like an acre of ground; not used, so the film never mixes them). Capital AICR here; lower-case aicr (hostnames, 'ssh aicr', the alias) is the next entry.
Lower-case aicr inside hostnames and commands (login.aicr.ai, ssh aicr, the aicr alias). Same four letters as the capital entry, so the film says it one way. Bear, 2026-10-11.

Godot: French-original go-DOH (/go.do/, even syllables, slight lean on the second; final t silent), chosen by Bear 2026-10-09 from four options (Beckett GOD-oh, US guh-DOH, French go-DOH, engine GO-dot). Kokoro defaults to GAH-daht ('God dot'). Voice only.

entries.note: In the BOUT title 'Agentic Coding Is Mostly Design', Kokoro says 'coating' (KOH-ting). Respelling 'co-ding' separates the syllables explicitly: 'co' (like co-author, /koʊ/) + 'ding' (the known word, /dɪŋ/) → kˈoʊdɪŋ. Narrower than 'koding' and forces Kokoro's neural model to read through the hyphen. Narrow pattern: only fires between 'Agentic' and 'Is'. Added 2026-10-11 for Agentic Figma Film 1. Voice only; narration and captions retain 'Coding'.
'redoable' = re-DOO-able (re + do, like 'undoable'), not 're-DOH-able' (as in bread dough). Kokoro says dough. Requested 2026-10-10. Covers redoable and re-doable.

The local model server. Kokoro reads Ollama as 'ah-LAH-muh' (ɑːlˈɑːmə); the name starts 'oh-' (oh-LAH-muh). Added 2026-10-13 while building the local-LLM-on-Explorer lecture; check by ear on first use.
The container tool (formerly Singularity), said AP-tay-ner. Kokoro says 'AP-tih-ner' (ˈæptɪnɚ). Added 2026-10-13; check by ear on first use.
The Qwen model family. Kokoro spells it out as the letter Q plus 'wen' (kjˈuːwˈɛn). Said 'Kwen' here (the maker's own pronunciation is closer to 'chwen'; Bear to choose). Added 2026-10-13.
